sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Dumuzid** (*dumuzid*) ​— Shepherds, ‌Vegetation · Faithful ‌son — ​belongs to the ​Mesopotamian tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued under the ​domain "Shepherds, ‌Vegetation". The name ​means "Faithful ​son"[^1].

Dumuzid is ‌the Sumerian **shepherd ​made divine** ‌— the 'faithful ​son' whose ‌name joins *dumu* ​('son') and ​*zid* ('true, faithful, ​right'). He is ​the lord ​of the sheepfold, ‌the provider ​of milk and ‌wool, and ​the bridegroom of ‌Inanna in the ​sacred marriage ‌that guarantees the ​land's fertility. ‌Unlike the storm-gods ​who rule ​by force, Dumuzid ‌reigns through the ‌gentle goods ‌of the pasture: ​grass, water, ​flock, and the ‌cyclic return ​of vegetation.

His ​myth is also ‌the myth ​of **seasonal loss**. ​In the ‌*Descent of Inanna* ​he is ‌chosen to take ​the goddess's ​place in the ​underworld for half ​the year, ‌so that life ‌and death ​may alternate on ‌earth. Dumuzid ​is therefore not ​only the patron ‌of shepherds ‌but the archetype ‌of the ‌dying-and-rising vegetation god, ​mourned as ‌Tammuz across the ​ancient Near East.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ​the name as ‌**Dumuzid** and ​serves its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/dumuzid/). The restoration ‌needs no distinctive ​letters or ​diacritics its ASCII ​form would ‌lose, which places ​the name ‌in Tier 2. ​The plain ASCII ‌form *dumuzid* ​survives as a ‌modern convenience ‌imposed by the ​early domain-name ​system; the restoration, ​not the fallback, ​is the ‌form the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Cuneiform as ​**𒀭𒌉𒍣**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"Faithful ‌son"[^1].

The ​ASCII ​form ‌*dumuzid* survives ​only ‌because ​the early ‌domain-name ​system could ​not ​carry ​diacritics; it ​is ‌a ​technological compromise, ‌not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Dumuzid** ‌recovers ​the full ​diacritic ‌detail of ‌the ‌scholarly ​transliteration directly ​in ‌the ​address bar. ​The ‌restoration needs ​no ​distinctive ‌letters or ​diacritics ‌its ​ASCII form ​would ​lose, which ​places ‌the ‌name in ​Tier ‌2.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ‌**d** ‌→ ‌**D** — ​Same, ‌capitalized
​- **u** ​→ ​**u** — ‌Same
​- ​**m** → ​**m** ‌— ​Same
- ​**u** ​→ **u** ‌— ​Same
‌- **z** ​→ ‌**z** ​— Same
‌- ‌**i** → ​**i** ​— ​Same
- ​**d** ‌→ ‌**d** — ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name ‌is **/duˈmu.zid/** ​— Sumerian/Akkadian Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ​**Du-** — ​Voiced alveolar stop ‌[d] plus ​close back ​rounded vowel ‌[u]; the Sumerian ​word dumu ‌means 'son'.
​- **-mu-** ‌— Bilabial nasal ​[m] plus ​close back ​rounded vowel ​[u]; the second ​syllable carries ‌the reconstructed ​stress.
- ‌**-zid** — Voiced ​alveolar fricative ‌[z] plus ​voiceless dental ‌stop [d]; zid ​means 'true, ‌faithful, right' ​— the ​ethical core of ‌the name.

‌For the ‌modern speaker, ​the closest approximation ​is: 'doo-MOO-zid' ‌— the ​first two ​syllables are soft ‌and round, ​the last ​closes crisply ‌like 'zid'.

Kindred ​and historical ‌forms of ​the name:

​- **Sumerian** — ​𒌉𒍣 (dumu-zid), ​'faithful son', ‌often written ‌with the divine ​determinative 𒀭
‌- **Akkadian** ​— Tammūzu, ​the East Semitic ‌form attested ‌from the ‌Old Akkadian ‌period onward
- ​**Hebrew/Biblical** — ‌Tammuz (תַּמּוּז), ​mourned at ​the Jerusalem temple ​gate in ‌Ezekiel 8:14

​Dumuzid is ​Tier 2: the ​canonical restoration ‌uses plain ​Latin letters ​with no distinctive ​diacritic or ‌non-ASCII letter. ​The Sumerian ‌cuneiform signs carry ​meanings — ‌dumu 'son' ​and zid ‌'faithful' — that ‌the Latin ​form cannot ​display; it ​is therefore a ​readable scholarly ‌transliteration rather ‌than a ​phonological reconstruction.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved ‌in Cuneiform ​as **𒀭𒌉𒍣**.[^1]

​The ​scholarly transliteration ​is ​*Dumuzid*.

The ‌rendering ​proceeds step ​by ‌step:

- ​The divine ‌determinative ​𒀭 (dingir) ‌marks ​Dumuzi as ​a ​deity
- ​𒌉 ​(DUMU) means ‌'son, child'
​- ‌𒍣 (ZI) ​means ‌'faithful, true, ​life'
‌- DUMU.ZI ​is ‌read Dumuzid, ​'faithful son', ​attested ‌from Early ‌Dynastic ‌texts and ​the ​Sumerian King ‌List

​The name ​is written ‌in ​Sumerian cuneiform ​as ‌𒌉𒍣 (*dumu-zid*), ​often ‌preceded by ​the ​divine determinative ​𒀭. The ​first ‌sign means ‌'son,' ​the second ‌'true, ​faithful, right.' ​Standard ‌Assyriology transliterates ‌the name ‌as ‌Dumuzi(d), with ​the ‌final -d ​sometimes ​omitted in ​older ‌spellings. Because ​the Latin ​form ​preserves no ‌distinctive ​diacritic or ​non-ASCII ​letter, it ‌is ​classified as ‌Tier 2: ​the ‌restoration is ​the ‌plain scholarly ‌transliteration, ​readable but ​stripped ​of the ​visual density ‌of ‌the original ​signs.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Dumuzid is ​the Sumerian ‌**shepherd made divine** ‌— the ​'faithful son' whose ​name joins *dumu* ​('son') and ​*zid* ('true, faithful, ​right'). He ‌is the lord ​of the ​sheepfold, the provider ‌of milk ​and wool, and ‌the bridegroom of ​Inanna in ‌the sacred marriage ​that guarantees ​the land's fertility. ​Unlike the ​storm-gods who rule ​by force, ‌Dumuzid reigns through ​the gentle goods ‌of the ​pasture: grass, water, ‌flock, and ​the cyclic return ‌of vegetation.

​His myth is ‌also the ​myth of **seasonal ​loss**. In the ‌*Descent of ‌Inanna* he is ‌chosen to ​take the goddess's ​place in ‌the underworld for ​half the ​year, so that ‌life and death ​may alternate ​on earth. Dumuzid ‌is therefore ​not only the ‌patron of ​shepherds but the ​archetype of the ​dying-and-rising vegetation ​god, mourned as ‌Tammuz across ‌the ancient Near ​East.[^1]

### ‌Lord of the ​Sheepfold

Patron ​of shepherds, milk, ‌cheese, and wool; ‌the pastoral ‌economy of Sumer ‌consecrated in ​one figure.

### ‌Date Palm ​and Garden

His ​wedding songs ​praise the date ‌palm, the garden, ​and the ​sprouting reed — ​the green ‌world as bridal ​gift.

### ​Sacred Marriage

The ​union of ‌Dumuzid and Inanna ​legitimates kingship and ‌assures fertility; ​every New Year ‌reenacts their ​cosmic wedding.

### ‌Descent and ‌Return

Half the ​year in ​the underworld, half ​on earth with ​his sister ‌Geshtinanna — the ‌seasonal cycle ​made myth.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Dumuzid ​concentrates ​in a ​small ​set ​of recurring ‌attributes, ​each ​a compressed ‌statement ​about ‌the ​name:[^1]

- ‌**Shepherd's ​crook** ​— The ​emblem ​of ​his pastoral ‌rule ​and ‌the surrogate ​kingship ‌enacted ​in ‌the sacred ​marriage
‌- ​**Milk pail ​and ‌churn** ‌— The ‌dairy ​abundance ​of the ‌flock; ​the ​goods ‌that win ​Inanna's ​hand ‌over the ​farmer's ‌grain
​- **Date ​palm** ​— ​The ‌sacred tree ‌of ​Inanna's ‌garden and ​the ​vegetative ‌power that ‌flourishes ‌in ‌Dumuzid's season
​- ‌**Wool ​and ​fleece** — ​The ‌textile ​wealth of ​the ​sheepfold ‌and the ​warm ​garment ​of the ‌bridegroom
​- ‌**Wedding ​ring** — ‌The ​sacred ‌marriage that ‌binds ​heaven ​and earth, ​goddess ​and ‌king, fertility ‌and ​legitimacy

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Dumuzid's myths ​are woven through the ‌great Sumerian literary ‌corpus: courtship songs, sacred-marriage ​hymns, the *Descent of ​Inanna*, and the ​laments for his death. ​They turn on ​the tension between abundance ‌and loss, intimacy ​and exile, the green ​world and the dark ‌earth.[^1]

### The ​Shepherd and the Farmer ‌(Courtship)

In the ​Sumerian poem *Dumuzi and ‌Enkimdu* (ETCSL 4.08.33), ​Inanna must choose between ​Dumuzid, the shepherd, and ​Enkimdu, the farmer. ​The shepherd boasts of ​milk, cheese, and ‌wool; the farmer counters ​with grain, bread, ‌and beer. Inanna prefers ​Dumuzid, and the ‌poem dramatizes the prestige ​of the pastoral economy ‌alongside agriculture in ​early Mesopotamia.[^2]

### The ‌Bridal of Heaven ​and Earth (Sacred Marriage)

​The sacred-marriage songs ‌(ETCSL 4.08.01–04) celebrate Dumuzid ‌as the bridegroom of ‌Inanna. The king ​of Uruk embodies Dumuzid, ​while the goddess ‌embodies the city and ​the land. Their ​union is not merely ‌symbolic: it guarantees the ​*me* of fertility, ​the sprouting of grain, ‌the filling of ​folds, and the legitimacy ‌of the reigning ​king.

### Dumuzid in ​the Underworld (Descent)

In ​the *Descent of ​Inanna* (ETCSL 1.4.1), Inanna ‌is killed in ‌the underworld and resurrected ​only on condition ‌that she send a ​substitute. She chooses Dumuzid, ​her beloved husband, ‌because he did not ‌mourn her. The ‌*galla* demons drag him ‌down, but his ​sister Geshtinanna offers to ‌share his fate: Dumuzid ​will spend half ​the year in the ​underworld, Geshtinanna the ‌other half. This is ​the Sumerian explanation ​of summer's parch and ​winter's return.

### ‌The Weeping for Tammuz ​(Lament)

Sumerian city laments ​(e.g., *The Death ​of Dumuzid*, ETCSL 4.08.32) ‌and later Akkadian ​tradition mourn the shepherd's ‌death. The biblical ​prophet Ezekiel witnesses women ‌'weeping for Tammuz' at ​the Jerusalem temple ‌gate (Ezekiel 8:14), a ‌rite that travelled ​from Mesopotamia to the ​Levant. The tears ​are not only grief; ​they are a petition ‌for the god's ‌return and the restoration ​of vegetation.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Dumuzid ​is ‌the Sumerian ‌original ​behind ​the ​Akkadian **Tammūzu** ​and ​the ‌later ​West Semitic ​Tammuz. ‌The ​Greeks ‌knew ​a comparable ‌dying-and-rising ​vegetation ​figure ​in **Adonis**; ​while ​Adonis ‌has ​separate Northwest ‌Semitic ​roots, ‌the ​two share ‌the ​same ‌seasonal ​logic and ​were ‌sometimes ‌identified ‌in ​later antiquity. ​In ‌the ​Hebrew ​Bible, Tammuz ‌appears ​as ​a ‌foreign deity ​mourned ‌in ​Jerusalem ​(Ezekiel 8:14), ​and ​the ‌month ‌Tammuz still ​bears ‌his ​name ​in ‌the Jewish ‌calendar. ‌Some ‌Sumerian ​god-lists distinguish ‌Dumuzid ​the ​Shepherd ​from Dumuzid-abzu, ‌a ​chthonic ​or ​freshwater form; ‌the ​traditions ​converged ​over time.[^1]

‌Within ​the ‌Mesopotamian ​tradition, ‌closely related ​names ‌in ‌the ​corpus include ​[[adad|Adad]], ​[[anu|Anû]], ​[[apsu|Apsû]], ‌[[ashur|Aššur]], [[ea|Ēa]], ‌and ​[[enkidu|Enkidu]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: The ​name ‌**Tammuz** ‌outlived ​Mesopotamian cult ​by ​millennia. ​The ​fourth ‌month ​of ​the ‌Jewish ​calendar, *Tammuz*, ‌preserves ​his ‌memory, ​and ​the ​fast ​of ​the ‌Seventeenth of ​Tammuz ‌commemorates ​national ‌calamity. ​In ‌Arabic ​and ‌Syriac ​folklore, Tammuz ​remained ‌a ‌byword ‌for ​the ​death ‌of ​vegetation ​and the ‌summer ​drought. ​Modern ‌scholarship ​treats ‌Dumuzid ​as ​a classic ​example ​of ‌the ‌'dying ​god' ‌type ​alongside ​Osiris, ‌Attis, and ‌Adonis ‌— ‌though ​each ‌figure ​has ​distinct ​local ‌roots. His ​myth ​still ​shapes ‌how ​we ​imagine ​the ‌cycle ​of seasons, ‌the ​return ‌of ​spring, ‌and ‌the ​intimate ​link ​between divine ​love ‌and ‌agricultural ​fertility.[^1]

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Dumuzid ​is the ‌god ‌who must ​be ​lost so ​that ​the world ​can ‌turn. His ​death ​is not ‌punishment for ​a ‌moral fault ​but ‌the structural ​price ​of Inanna's ​return ​from the ​underworld. ‌In choosing ​him, ‌the goddess ​does ‌not act ​out ‌of cruelty; ​she ‌acts out ​of ​the logic ‌that life ‌and ‌death must ​alternate, ​that the ‌green ​world must ​descend ‌into darkness ​in ​order to ‌rise ​again.

To ‌meditate ​on Dumuzid ​is ​to meditate ​on ‌the beloved ‌thing ​that disappears. ‌The ​pasture dries, ​the flock ‌is ‌penned, the ‌bridegroom ‌is taken ​underground ‌— and ​yet ​the cycle ​guarantees ‌return. His ​sister's ​compassion, splitting ​the ‌sentence, reminds ​us ​that exile ​is ‌bearable when ​it ‌is shared. ​Dumuzid asks: ‌what ​in your ‌life ‌must die ​for ​half a ​year ​so that ‌the ‌rest may ​live?[^1]
